title: Godland (2022): They got us in the first half

commenti.body:
>where we see the demise of Lucas.

Yeah, what was with his death? It just sort of comes out of left field. Like, what is Carl's motivation, exactly? I understand he dislikes Lucas for a variety of reasons: resentment of Danish colonialism, Lucas's interest in his daughter, Anna, and the horse stealing, but are any of those reasons enough to stab a man to death?

The only other thing I could think of is maybe Carl saw Ragnar's dog, thought it strange he would leave it behind and then, with Luca's abrupt fleeing, puts two and two together and kills Lucas out of revenge.

Whatever the reason, it did feel quite unexpected.

I thought it was an amazing film. It reminded me of Sorsese's silence done in a Bergmanesque manner but with that brilliant 'non fiction fiction' trope that we see in the film 'Fargo' (i.e. - the photos). .....and I think in this  sense the Director leans towards the "This bit is obviously teasing with the truth so maybe it all is". I don't know about you but I googled the photos as soon as the film finished.

Now this might sound trite and whimsy, and I'd normally not go for such a cocnept to be honest (does it add anything?) but I think it was just directed so well and I was so engaged in it all that I bought into it.

I think it’s pretty close to perfect (at least going by the slipping standards of modern filmmaking), but I do agree that the first half is stronger than the second. I felt the pacing was just ever so slightly off in the second half. However, the only part that was truly weak to me in how contrived it was the (pretty big spoilers here) reveal that Ragnar killed Lucas’ horse, which seemed very out-of-character for him and merely functioned to initiate the dramatic fight scene.

I don’t think you are wrong to have that opinion. Different things work for different people. For me it all worked though. Got some Aguirre, the Wrath of God vibes and Diary of a Country Priest vibes as well. And I really liked the silence in this film. The long zoom outs that emphasize the enormity of the natural landscapes. The harshness of nature and how disconnected from the land and foolish the priest and his religion are in face of that. It is pretty obvious as far as themes. For me that’s not necessarily a bad thing though. Plus those 360 degree shots are to die for.

It is exceptionally well directed and even though I complaint about stuff in my post, I admit I enjoyed watching the whole thing. There is a sequence near the end where we see the subjects posing in front of the camera, I guess as if the camera is Lucas’ POV; those were greaaaat
True, that reveal was kinda out of nowhere. And Ragnar was such a great character up to that point. You see him powerful and dominant in the first half and then clumsy and out of place in the second.

I didn't mind the contrast in his character. I don't think he's so much clumsy as just drunk due to feeling condescended and ostracised in civilisation. He's meant to be a direct contrast to Lucas in being connected to the landscape and the truer essences of the world than the constructed meaning Lucas thrives on (which see being literally constructed as the church is built), which is why I feel the killing of the horse felt so severely out of character for him.
